chapter_theme: The ten of துவ்வாப் பத்து set ten things that look like goods (wealth, daring, a life, a gift, an undertaking, help, a bond, a companion, old age, pleasure) each against a plain lack or a vice and find them no better, so that each good is emptied by the fault that comes with it: blame, excess, shamelessness, disregard, failure to act, falsity, ingratitude, folly, disgrace and not sharing.

31.reading: The wealth of those who carry blame is reckoned no better than poverty.
31.nuance: Line 1 is the frame of the whole ten, so the saying of 31 is line 2 alone. துவ்வாது is read through the ten as 'does not rise above'; the verb's plain sense is to eat or enjoy, so the wealth that is 'no better than poverty' is also wealth that cannot really be enjoyed. Here the comparison word is வறுமையில், with -இல், where the other nine have -இன்.

items.claim: the wealth of the blameworthy is no better than want

32.reading: Reckless daring that goes beyond measure is reckoned no better than the state of a பேடி.
32.nuance: The printed கழிதறு கண்மை is கழி + தறுகண்மை split by the line's spacing: not daring itself but daring in excess. பேடி is a gender word for one neither man nor woman, used in the period as the type of the man without courage; the saying turns that type against the over-bold, so the two extremes meet.

items.claim: excessive daring is no better than being a பேடி

33.reading: A life without shame is reckoned no better than going hungry.
33.nuance: The measure is bodily want: whatever such a life has to eat, it is counted as a hungry one, which is the force of துவ்வாது (it does not eat or enjoy).

items.claim: a shameless life is no better than hunger

34.reading: Giving done without care for the receiver is reckoned no better than refusing.
34.nuance: பேணில் is read as பேணு + இல், giving without cherishing or honouring the one who receives; the manner of the gift cancels the gift.

items.claim: a gift given without regard is no better than a refusal

35.reading: Taking a task upon oneself and not doing it is reckoned no better than being a dullard.
35.nuance: செய்யாமை மேற்கோள் is read as an undertaking (மேற்கோள்) marked by not-doing; it could also be read as taking up the vow of not acting, which would make it idleness rather than a broken undertaking. சிதடி means a fool and also one who is blind.

items.claim: an undertaking left undone is no better than stupidity

36.reading: False benevolence, help that is only a show, is reckoned no better than baseness.
36.nuance: பொய்வே ளாண்மை is பொய் + வேளாண்மை split by the spacing. The measure புலைமை is formed from புலை, a birth-group term of the period that ranks people as low; here it names baseness as a quality, and the saying states no rule about persons, but the word's caste sense lies under the comparison.

items.claim: pretended helpfulness is no better than baseness

37.reading: Turning one's regard away from those one has taken from is reckoned no better than cruelty.
37.nuance: கொண்டு may mean having received a benefit or having taken someone as one's own (a friend, a dependant); either way கண்மாறல், turning the eye away, names the breach of a bond already accepted, which is ingratitude rather than mere unkindness.

items.claim: to receive and then withdraw one's regard is no better than cruelty

38.reading: The company and support of a fool is reckoned no better than being alone.

items.claim: a fool's support is no better than solitude

39.reading: Old age that has fallen into disgrace is reckoned no better than anger, on the most direct reading of கதம்.
39.nuance: கதம் most often means anger or heat of temper, and the comparison of a disgraced old age to anger is hard to see; the word may carry another sense here (a sting, a hurt), so the measure of this saying cannot be fixed.

items.claim: a degraded old age is no better than கதம்

40.reading: Enjoying pleasure by oneself alone is reckoned no better than solitude.
40.nuance: The same measure, தனிமை, closes 38: unshared joy is counted as the very loneliness the solitary man suffers, so pleasure kept to oneself is no pleasure.

items.claim: enjoying pleasure alone is no better than loneliness

links.note: Kural 657 sets the utter poverty of the worthy above wealth won under blame; Muthumozhikkanchi 31 sets the wealth of the blameworthy level with poverty.
links.teaches: The couplet ranks clean poverty above tainted wealth, while the line only levels them, and holding both shows a scale with two steps: tainted wealth is already worth no more than want, and the worthy man's want is worth more still.
links.list_adds: It makes tainted wealth one of ten things measured against a plain lack (hunger, solitude, refusal), so blame is shown to empty wealth of what wealth is for, not merely to rank below virtue.

links.note: Kural 773 calls தறுகண் great manliness and gives it kindness to the fallen foe as its edge; the line says that தறுகண்மை in excess (கழி) is no better than the பேடி's lack of it.
links.teaches: The Kural refines valour by adding mercy as its edge, and the line limits it by measure, so the pair shows two separate checks on courage: mercy to the fallen and restraint in excess.
links.list_adds: Set in a ten where each thing is equated with its seeming opposite, it makes the over-bold and the coward one kind, a turn the couplet's praise of valour does not make.

links.note: Kural 1012 says food and clothing are common to all living beings and shame is the mark of humans; the line says a life without shame is no better than hunger.
links.teaches: The couplet sets shame above food as what makes a person human; the line turns the same order into a verdict on the shameless man, whose full table counts for no more than an empty one.
links.list_adds: It measures the lack of shame in the coin of food, the very thing the couplet put aside as common to all, so the ranking is applied as a judgement on a life rather than stated as a definition.

links.note: Naladiyar 268 sees the shameless feasting at home while those with shame walk far and eat scraps; the line counts a shameless life as no better than hunger.
links.teaches: The quatrain records the outward fact that shamelessness feeds well, and the line answers it by counting that full stomach as hunger, so together they give the complaint and its reply.
links.list_adds: The line states as a measure what the quatrain shows as a scene, setting the shameless life among ten counterfeit goods that equal their lacks.

links.note: Kural 1057 says the asker rejoices deep within on meeting givers who do not scorn; the line says giving without regard is no better than withholding.
links.teaches: The couplet locates the worth of a gift in the asker's inner joy at being spared scorn, and the line draws the conclusion from the giver's side: without that regard the gift is as good as refused.
links.list_adds: It puts the careless gift beside the shameless life and the false helper, ten things that keep the outward form of a good while lacking its substance, which the couplet, focused on the asker, does not do.

links.note: Kural 664 says speaking is easy for all and doing as one said is hard; the line counts an undertaking left undone as no better than folly.
links.teaches: The couplet names the gap between word and deed as a difficulty, and the line names its cost to the man who leaves it open: he is counted a fool, so failure to perform becomes a matter of judgement, not only of strength.
links.list_adds: By measuring the broken undertaking against சிதடி, it moves the couplet's point from firmness in action to the standing of the one who fails, among other things judged as their opposites.

links.note: Kural 110 says there is no escape for one who kills a good done to him; the line counts withdrawing regard after receiving as no better than cruelty.
links.teaches: The couplet ranks ingratitude as the sin without remedy, and the line names what it is in act: the ungrateful man, who strikes no one, is reckoned as cruel as one who does harm.
links.list_adds: It classes ingratitude with கொடுமை, an act of harm, where the couplet ranks it among sins by its consequence, so the list says what kind of wrong it is rather than how grave.

links.note: Kural 816 says being a stranger to the wise is ten million times better than close friendship with a fool; the line counts a fool's support as no better than solitude.
links.teaches: The couplet sinks the fool's friendship far below even estrangement from the wise, while the line only equates it with having no one, and the pair shows the range of the same judgement from mild to extreme.
links.list_adds: It measures the fool's company against solitude, the measure the same ten uses for unshared pleasure in 40, so a bad companion and a joy kept to oneself are shown to leave a person equally alone.

links.note: Both lines close on தனிமையின் துவ்வாது: a fool's support and pleasure enjoyed alone are each no better than solitude.
links.teaches: Read together, the two make solitude the measure from both sides: one may be alone though accompanied, by a fool, or alone though joyful, by not sharing, so company is defined by what is shared and not by who is present.

links.note: Kural 229 says eating alone to fill one's own store is more bitter than begging; the line says enjoying pleasure alone is no better than solitude.
links.teaches: The couplet ranks solitary eating below begging, a loss of goods and honour, while the line counts any unshared pleasure as loneliness, so the pair shows the same fault judged once as social shame and once as the self's own isolation.
links.list_adds: It widens the couplet's solitary eating to every pleasure kept to oneself and pairs it within the ten with the fool's company, both measured by solitude.

source_issues: 31: the comparison site's text lacks line 2 (பழியோர் செல்வம் வறுமையில் துவ்வாது), the saying itself; our text has it after the frame line.
31: வறுமையில் has the -இல் ending where the other nine lines of the ten have -இன் before துவ்வாது; possibly a variant or misprint for வறுமையின்.
32, 36: the printed spacing splits words across sandhi (கழிதறு கண்மை for கழி தறுகண்மை, பொய்வே ளாண்மை for பொய் வேளாண்மை).
39: கதத்தின் is the comparison word; its sense in this line is doubtful.
